items.prompt: What is a "brag doc"?
choices: A running, personal log of work completed and its impact, updated regularly so nothing has to be reconstructed from memory later
A document a manager writes about an employee without their input
A formal complaint filed to request a promotion
A resume submitted to external companies
items.explanation: A brag doc is a personal, ongoing record — its value is specifically that it's updated close to when the work happened, rather than reconstructed later from memory.
items.reference:
📓 Brag doc — personal, running, updated regularly
🚫 Not — a one-time document written at review time

Why: the timing (running log vs. after-the-fact reconstruction) is what makes a brag doc actually useful.

items.prompt: Why does a brag doc need to be updated regularly, rather than written all at once during a review cycle?
choices: Because specific details and numbers fade from memory quickly — capturing them close to when the work happened preserves detail a later reconstruction would lose
Because company policy typically requires weekly documentation
Because regular updates are faster to write than one long document
Because reviews only accept documents updated within the last week
items.explanation: The whole value of a running log is capturing detail while it's fresh — writing it all at review time reconstructs from memory just as unreliably as a manager would.
items.reference:
📓 Brag doc — personal, running, updated regularly
🚫 Not — a one-time document written at review time

Why: the timing (running log vs. after-the-fact reconstruction) is what makes a brag doc actually useful.

items.prompt: What is "visibility," as this unit defines it?
choices: The degree to which the people who make decisions about your career actually know what you've done — distinct from whether the work itself was good
How many people follow your work updates on an internal chat tool
The size of your monitor or number of screens you use while working
How often your manager schedules one-on-one meetings with you
items.explanation: Visibility is specifically about decision-makers' awareness of your work — the opening scenario shows good work with low visibility failing to produce a strong promotion case, precisely because of this gap.
items.reference:
💎 Good work — one thing
👁️ Visibility — a separate thing: does anyone who matters know about it?

Why: conflating these two is exactly why "the work should speak for itself" fails as a strategy.

items.prompt: Why does this unit treat "visibility" as separate from "doing good work"?
choices: Because the two can diverge — the opening scenario's bug fix was genuinely good work with almost no visibility, which is exactly what caused the thin promotion packet
Because visibility is more important than the actual quality of the work
Because good work is always automatically visible to decision-makers
Because visibility only applies to junior employees
items.explanation: The opening scenario is built around exactly this gap — real, valuable work with low visibility, demonstrating that the two are genuinely separate properties.
items.reference:
💎 Good work — one thing
👁️ Visibility — a separate thing: does anyone who matters know about it?

Why: conflating these two is exactly why "the work should speak for itself" fails as a strategy.

items.prompt: What is "self-promotion anxiety"?
choices: The discomfort of documenting your own work, often rooted in a fear that stating facts about your own impact will be read as boasting
A clinical anxiety disorder requiring professional treatment
The fear of public speaking in front of large audiences
Nervousness specifically about asking for a raise in a one-on-one meeting
items.explanation: Self-promotion anxiety is the specific discomfort tied to documenting one's own work — the unit's core claim is that this discomfort tracks how the facts are framed, not the facts themselves.
items.reference:
😬 The discomfort — fear that stating facts reads as boasting
🔍 What it actually tracks — subjective framing, not the facts themselves

Why: understanding what the discomfort is actually about is the key to resolving it, per L2.

items.prompt: According to this unit, is self-promotion anxiety usually about the underlying facts themselves, or about how those facts are typically stated?
choices: How the facts are typically stated — the discomfort tracks subjective self-assessment, not objective description
The underlying facts themselves, which are inherently embarrassing to state
Neither — the anxiety has no identifiable cause
Company policy, which technically forbids discussing one's own work
items.explanation: L2 is explicit: the discomfort tracks subjective claims like "I did a great job," not the objective facts of what happened — this is the basis for the entire objective-framing solution.
items.reference:
😬 The discomfort — fear that stating facts reads as boasting
🔍 What it actually tracks — subjective framing, not the facts themselves

Why: understanding what the discomfort is actually about is the key to resolving it, per L2.

items.prompt: What is "objective framing"?
choices: Describing impact in terms of what happened and what changed, rather than subjective self-assessment
Writing about a project using only technical jargon
Having a manager write the description instead of the employee
Removing all numbers and specifics from a description to keep it neutral
items.explanation: Objective framing reports what happened and what changed (a fact the reader can evaluate independently), rather than delivering a verdict about the writer's own quality.
items.reference:
❌ "I did a great job" — subjective verdict
✅ "Cut latency from 400ms to 60ms" — objective fact

Why: this is the specific technique that resolves self-promotion anxiety, per L2's central argument.

items.prompt: Which of these is an example of objective framing, per this unit?
choices: "Led the database migration; cut query latency from 400ms to 60ms with zero downtime."
"I did a great job leading the migration."
"I clearly demonstrated senior-level ownership on this project."
"This shows I'm ready for more responsibility."
items.explanation: The first option states a concrete fact about what happened and what changed — the other three are all subjective judgments the writer is making about their own quality.
items.reference:
❌ "I did a great job" — subjective verdict
✅ "Cut latency from 400ms to 60ms" — objective fact

Why: this is the specific technique that resolves self-promotion anxiety, per L2's central argument.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, why did the promotion packet end up thin despite the engineer's real, valuable work?
choices: The manager's memory, six months later, could clearly recall a recent flashy demo but not the quiet bug fix or other work done in between
The engineer's work was actually low-quality and didn't deserve documentation
The company had a policy against documenting bug fixes
The manager deliberately excluded the bug fix out of favoritism toward other engineers
items.explanation: The scenario's point is specifically about the limits of unaided memory — recent, dramatic, or personally-witnessed work survives, while quiet, competent work fades, regardless of its actual value.
items.reference:
🛠️ What happened — a nasty bug fixed quietly, no fanfare
🧠 What the manager remembers — a demo from two months ago

Why: this is the exact mechanism the unit addresses — good work with no record, filtered through unreliable memory.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario's closing question, whose "fault" is the thin promotion packet — the manager's memory, or something the engineer could have controlled?
choices: Something the engineer could have controlled — keeping their own running record, rather than relying entirely on the manager's memory
Entirely the manager's fault, since managers should have perfect recall of all their reports' work
Nobody's fault — promotion packets are inherently random
The company's fault for not requiring managers to take detailed notes
items.explanation: The unit's framing isn't about blaming the manager's memory (which is a genuinely unreliable archive for anyone) — it's about the engineer having a lever they didn't use: keeping their own record.
items.reference:
🛠️ What happened — a nasty bug fixed quietly, no fanfare
🧠 What the manager remembers — a demo from two months ago

Why: this is the exact mechanism the unit addresses — good work with no record, filtered through unreliable memory.

items.prompt: According to L2's flowchart, what kind of work "survives" in a manager's memory by the time a promotion cycle happens?
choices: Vivid, recent, or personally-witnessed work — not necessarily the most valuable or representative work
Only the work that was formally logged in a project management tool
Whichever work took the longest number of hours
All work equally, regardless of when it happened or how it was witnessed
items.explanation: L2's flowchart is explicit that only vivid, recent, or personally-witnessed work survives unaided memory — a selection process that has nothing to do with actual value or representativeness.
items.reference:
🧠 Unaided memory — favors vivid, recent, witnessed work
📓 Brag doc — captures the full record, regardless of memorability

Why: a brag doc doesn't replace the work — it replaces the manager's memory as the record of it.

items.prompt: What does L2 say a brag doc actually replaces?
choices: The manager's memory as the record of the work — not the work itself
The need to actually do good work in the first place
The performance review process entirely
The engineer's manager, who becomes unnecessary once a brag doc exists
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that a brag doc doesn't replace doing the work — it replaces relying on someone else's unaided memory as the only record of that work.
items.reference:
🧠 Unaided memory — favors vivid, recent, witnessed work
📓 Brag doc — captures the full record, regardless of memorability

Why: a brag doc doesn't replace the work — it replaces the manager's memory as the record of it.

items.prompt: According to L2's comparison table, how does subjective self-assessment "read," compared to objective framing?
choices: Subjective self-assessment reads as advocacy (asking the reader to agree); objective framing reads as analysis (giving the reader something to evaluate)
Both read identically to any reader, regardless of phrasing
Subjective self-assessment always reads as more persuasive than objective framing
Objective framing always reads as cold and impersonal, which readers dislike
items.explanation: L2's table draws this exact distinction — advocacy asks for agreement, while analysis presents evaluable facts, which is why objective framing avoids the discomfort of self-promotion.
items.reference:
SubjectiveObjective
Reads asAdvocacyAnalysis

Why: this distinction is the mechanism behind why objective framing resolves self-promotion anxiety instead of just disguising the same claim.

items.prompt: Why does L2 say objective framing genuinely resolves the discomfort of self-promotion, rather than just disguising the same underlying claim?
choices: Because it's actually a different claim — a fact the reader can independently judge, not a verdict the writer is asking the reader to accept about themselves
Because objective framing is technically a lie, so it doesn't count as self-promotion
Because readers never notice the difference between the two framings
Because objective framing always uses fewer words than subjective framing
items.explanation: L2 explicitly argues this is a genuine difference in what's being claimed, not just a rhetorical trick — stating a fact and asking the reader to judge it is a different act than asserting your own quality.
items.reference:

Why: this distinction is the mechanism behind why objective framing resolves self-promotion anxiety instead of just disguising the same claim.

items.prompt: L2 lists three things a useful brag doc entry needs beyond just a title. Which of these is one of them?
choices: What was hard about it — the judgment calls or ambiguity navigated, which is usually what makes an entry worth documenting at all
The exact time of day the work was completed
A list of every tool or programming language mentioned anywhere in the codebase
A comparison to a specific coworker's performance
items.explanation: "What was hard about it" is one of L2's three elements (alongside "what changed" and "why it mattered") — it's what distinguishes brag-doc-worthy work from routine tasks.
items.reference:
1️⃣ What changed — concrete before/after
2️⃣ Why it mattered — the actual stakes
3️⃣ What was hard — the judgment calls involved

Why: a title alone ("fixed a bug") loses exactly the detail that makes an entry useful six months later.

items.prompt: Why does L2 say "what was hard about it" belongs in a brag doc entry?
choices: Because it's usually what makes the entry worth documenting at all — routine work usually isn't brag-doc material, but the judgment calls involved usually are
Because difficulty is the only thing promotion committees ever look at
Because it makes the entry sound more impressive regardless of what actually happened
Because company policy requires stating a difficulty level for every task
items.explanation: L2 frames "what was hard" as the distinguishing factor between routine work and work worth logging — it's what a reader (or future self) needs to recognize the judgment involved.
items.reference:
1️⃣ What changed — concrete before/after
2️⃣ Why it mattered — the actual stakes
3️⃣ What was hard — the judgment calls involved

Why: a title alone ("fixed a bug") loses exactly the detail that makes an entry useful six months later.

items.prompt: L2's failure modes list warns against writing brag doc entries only at review time. What's the specific consequence?
choices: By review time, most of the specific numbers and context are already gone — the entry ends up reconstructed from memory just as unreliably as the manager's version
Review-time entries are automatically rejected by most companies' HR systems
It takes exactly the same amount of time regardless of when it's written
It causes the engineer to be seen as less collaborative by their team
items.explanation: This defeats the entire purpose of a running log — reconstructing detail from memory at review time has the same failure mode as relying on a manager's memory in the first place.
items.reference:
❌ Write at review time — detail already lost, same failure as manager's memory
✅ Write close to the work — detail still fresh

Why: the timing of writing is what actually makes a brag doc more reliable than memory — not just having one at all.

items.prompt: Why does L2 say writing a brag doc entry "just as badly" as a manager's memory can happen even with a brag doc in place?
choices: If the entry is written months after the fact, at review time, it suffers the same memory decay a manager's unaided recollection would — having a document doesn't help if it's written too late
Brag docs are inherently unreliable regardless of when they're written
Managers always ignore brag docs no matter when they're written
Written documents decay in accuracy faster than human memory does
items.explanation: The mechanism (detail loss over time) is the same whether it's a manager's memory or a late-written brag doc entry — the tool only helps if used with the right cadence.
items.reference:
❌ Write at review time — detail already lost, same failure as manager's memory
✅ Write close to the work — detail still fresh

Why: the timing of writing is what actually makes a brag doc more reliable than memory — not just having one at all.

items.prompt: In L3's "Version A" draft ("Wasn't a big deal, just needed to look into it"), what's the specific problem?
choices: It's under-described — a reader six months later has no idea what actually happened, how bad it was, or what skill it demonstrated
It contains a factual lie about what happened
It's too long and should be shortened further
It uses too many technical terms a non-engineer wouldn't understand
items.explanation: L3 diagnoses Version A as stripping out exactly the facts that matter — modesty in phrasing that actively undersells real, judgment-call debugging work.
items.reference:
📝 Version A — "wasn't a big deal" — strips out the facts that matter
📝 Version B — "clearly demonstrates senior-level ownership" — adds a verdict that isn't the writer's to give

Why: both are miscalibrated in opposite directions — one under-describes, one over-claims.

items.prompt: L3 says Version A and Version B are "both just badly calibrated," not that one is more honest than the other. What does this mean?
choices: Neither version is dishonest — one strips out facts that matter, the other adds a verdict that isn't the writer's to give; both fail for different reasons, not because either one lies
Version A is completely honest and Version B is a complete lie
Both versions are equally dishonest and equally useless
There is no meaningful difference between the two versions at all
items.explanation: L3 explicitly frames this as a calibration problem in both directions, not an honesty problem — neither version states a falsehood, but neither gives a reader what they need either.
items.reference:
📝 Version A — "wasn't a big deal" — strips out the facts that matter
📝 Version B — "clearly demonstrates senior-level ownership" — adds a verdict that isn't the writer's to give

Why: both are miscalibrated in opposite directions — one under-describes, one over-claims.

items.prompt: In L3's objective-framing rewrite, what specifically states "why it mattered" without the writer directly claiming credit?
choices: "No customer-facing incident was ever declared because it was caught and fixed before support tickets started coming in" — stating the stakes as a fact, not a claim
"This shows I'm ready for more responsibility"
"I saved the company from a major disaster"
The rewrite doesn't address why the work mattered at all
items.explanation: L3 specifically points to this line as stating the stakes (what could have happened) as an objective fact, letting the reader infer the significance rather than the writer asserting it directly.
items.reference:
✅ What changed — "2% of customer records," "3 weeks," "new invariant check"
✅ Why it mattered — "no incident was ever declared" — stakes stated as fact
✅ What was hard — diagnosing an uncaught bug via log correlation

Why: this rewrite hits all three of L2's elements without a single subjective self-assessment.

items.prompt: What is explicitly absent from L3's objective-framing rewrite, compared to Version B?
choices: Any phrase like "I did a great job" or "this shows I'm ready for promotion" — no subjective self-assessment at all
Any mention of what the bug actually was
Any timeframe for how long the bug existed
Any description of the technical fix itself
items.explanation: L3 explicitly notes the absence of self-assessment phrases — the entry states facts and lets the reader draw conclusions, which L3 argues is a stronger endorsement than the writer's own claim.
items.reference:
✅ What changed — "2% of customer records," "3 weeks," "new invariant check"
✅ Why it mattered — "no incident was ever declared" — stakes stated as fact
✅ What was hard — diagnosing an uncaught bug via log correlation

Why: this rewrite hits all three of L2's elements without a single subjective self-assessment.

items.prompt: Per L3, why can a manager use the objective-framing entry "close to verbatim" in a promotion packet?
choices: The facts are already stated in a form a promotion committee (who never saw the work happen) can evaluate on their own
Because the manager is legally required to copy employee-submitted text exactly
Because the entry is written in the manager's own voice already
Because promotion committees only accept unedited employee submissions
items.explanation: L3's point is practical: an objectively-framed entry is already in a form a committee (with no first-hand knowledge) can evaluate, so the manager doesn't have to translate a vague or overclaiming entry into something usable.
items.reference:
😕 Vague entry — manager must reconstruct detail from hazy memory
😬 Overclaiming entry — manager must restate the writer's self-assessment as their own claim
✅ Objective entry — usable close to verbatim

Why: this is the practical payoff of objective framing — it's not just more comfortable to write, it's more useful to the person who has to use it later.

items.prompt: What two problems does a manager avoid when a brag doc entry is written with objective framing, per L3?
choices: Reconstructing detail from a hazy memory, AND having to restate the employee's own self-assessment as their own claim
Having to read the entry at all, and having to write anything themselves
Needing to know the employee's job title, and needing to know their team
Scheduling a meeting, and sending a follow-up email
items.explanation: L3 identifies both failure modes an objectively-framed entry avoids: it removes the need for memory reconstruction, and it removes the awkwardness of a manager having to adopt the employee's own self-assessment as their claim.
items.reference:
😕 Vague entry — manager must reconstruct detail from hazy memory
😬 Overclaiming entry — manager must restate the writer's self-assessment as their own claim
✅ Objective entry — usable close to verbatim

Why: this is the practical payoff of objective framing — it's not just more comfortable to write, it's more useful to the person who has to use it later.

items.prompt: L3's extend-it question asks how to apply objective framing to a mentoring conversation with no obvious before/after metric. What would a concrete, checkable version of "I helped a junior engineer grow" look like?
choices: Something like: what specific skill or blocker the mentoring addressed, and an observable change afterward — e.g. "after three pairing sessions on debugging strategy, they independently diagnosed and fixed the next two similar bugs without help"
There's no way to apply objective framing to mentoring — it should always stay vague
Simply repeating "I did a great job mentoring" more emphatically
Listing the number of meetings attended, regardless of what was discussed in them
items.explanation: This follows L2's three elements applied to a non-metric case: what changed (an observable behavior shift), why it mattered (independence on similar problems), and what was hard (identifying and addressing the specific gap) — concrete and checkable without needing a headline number.
items.reference:
📊 Bug fix — has natural metrics (records affected, time)
🤝 Mentoring — needs a different kind of concrete, checkable specific — an observable behavior change, not a fabricated number

Why: this is L3's own extend-it question — testing whether the reader can apply the general technique beyond the one worked example that happened to have clean metrics.

items.prompt: Why does L3 pose the mentoring extend-it question rather than assuming objective framing always needs a numeric metric like the bug-fix example?
choices: Because not every piece of work has a clean number, and forcing one where it doesn't exist would mean fabricating a metric — the reader should practice finding concrete, checkable specifics that aren't numbers
Because mentoring is outside the scope of career documentation entirely
Because numeric metrics are always more persuasive regardless of whether they're real
Because L3 believes mentoring conversations cannot be documented under any framework
items.explanation: This connects directly to L2's failure mode about not fabricating a metric that doesn't exist — the mentoring case is deliberately chosen because it forces the reader to find non-numeric but still concrete and checkable specifics.
items.reference:
📊 Bug fix — has natural metrics (records affected, time)
🤝 Mentoring — needs a different kind of concrete, checkable specific — an observable behavior change, not a fabricated number

Why: this is L3's own extend-it question — testing whether the reader can apply the general technique beyond the one worked example that happened to have clean metrics.
